# The Streets That Aren't There

Somewhere in the history of cartography, a mapmaker sat down and invented a street. He gave it a name, drew its curbs and its intersections, and placed it in a quiet corner of a city where no street had ever existed. He did this on purpose, and he hoped nobody would notice.

These invented streets are called trap streets, or copyright traps, and they are one of my favorite small deceptions in the history of human knowledge. The logic is simple. A mapmaker publishes a city guide. Rivals, who want to sell their own guides without paying for the surveying, copy the original. If the copier reproduces a street that appears nowhere else in the world, the copying is proven. The fake street is a fingerprint, a way of saying *this came from me*. Some of these phantom streets were absorbed so thoroughly into the maps that followed that they took on a second life. A fictional lane in one edition became a real address in the minds of people who lived nearby. In at least one famous case, a settlement was built on the name, and the village that grew there was called, roughly, "Agloe" after the made-up place on a map of New York State. It exists now as a tiny crossroads with a general store, and it is a town that began as a lie told to catch a thief.

I find this story irresistible, but I find it more irresistible the longer I think about it. A map is supposed to be a promise: here is the land, here is how it is arranged. We trust maps the way we trust few other documents. We fold them, mark them, hand them to strangers. And yet every map is a selection. It must leave out almost everything. A map of a city that showed every tree, every crack in the pavement, every person standing on every corner would be useless, a second city laid over the first, impossible to read. So the mapmaker decides, constantly, what matters, and what can be dropped. The trap street is the mapmaker's confession that the selection is a human act, that someone chose the lines, and that the lines can be false.

---

I have been thinking about maps lately partly because of how I learned to navigate as a child. My grandmother had a road atlas that lived in the glovebox of a car that smelled of peppermints and old upholstery. The atlas had been annotated over decades in three or four different pens. Some roads had been crossed out where highways had been rerouted. Some towns had circles drawn around them because they were where relatives lived, or where a particular diner was good, or where something had happened that nobody discussed. Reading that atlas was never just reading geography. It was reading a record of a woman's life, rendered in lines and marginalia. The official map was the skeleton, and her pen was the flesh.

This is, I think, the deeper truth behind the trap street. Every map is a collaboration between the authoritative and the personal. The printed lines claim to be objective, and in a sense they are; the rivers are where the rivers are. But the act of choosing what to draw, and what to name, and what to trust, is always partly a story. The mapmaker who invented a street was telling a story too, a story about the value of his own work and the fragility of other people's honesty.

---

There is a related idea in the way we handle information more generally. We tend to think of knowledge as a pile of facts that accumulate, each one either true or false, each one either attached to its source or floating free. But the trap street shows how fragile this picture is. Once a false thing enters the world, it does not stay where you put it. It gets copied, cited, printed in the next edition, asked about by a traveler who wants directions, and eventually it acquires the weight of reality simply through repetition. The fake street became a real place. The lie, once it had enough witnesses, became a fact on the ground.

I think about this when I encounter claims that seem obviously wrong but that have been repeated so often they feel familiar. Familiarity is a strange kind of evidence. We tend to believe things we have heard before, even when we cannot remember where we heard them. Psychologists have studied this under various names, the illusory truth effect among them: statements that are repeated become more credible, regardless of whether they are accurate. The mapmaker's trap worked on the same principle in reverse. He planted a fiction that was meant to be discovered as fiction, but the world's tendency to take in what it sees was stronger than his cleverness. The street survived because it looked like it belonged.

So what does it mean to be a careful reader of the world? Partly it means remembering that everything you know arrived through some channel, and that channels can carry things that are not there. Partly it means cultivating a gentle suspicion toward the too-convenient detail, the place name that sounds exactly like what you'd expect, the fact that confirms what you already hoped. Trap streets are often designed to sound plausible. They are named like real streets because their purpose is to be mistaken for real ones. The better the fake, the more it reveals about what we are willing to accept without checking.

---

I do not want to end on pure cynicism, though, because the trap street is also a kind of delight. Consider the people who found it. A surveyor in the field, perhaps, or a traveler with a map in one hand and a street sign in the other, looking for a road that was not there, and eventually concluding that the map was wrong. Or consider the copyists themselves, who must have felt a small thrill at seeing their own false street reproduced by a rival, and who perhaps did not realize until much later that they had been caught. Each of these moments is a tiny drama of discovery, the sudden reversal of trust.

And there is something almost tender about the mapmaker's invention. He had to imagine a place in complete detail, to decide what the street would be called, where it would bend, how wide it would be. He built a little world and then hid it inside the real one. In a sense, every novelist does this. Every map of an imagined country, every fictional town with its streets and churches and bakeries, is a kind of trap street that we agree to enter willingly. The difference is that the novelist tells us the street is invented. The mapmaker did not. The trap works only because the reader forgets to ask.

I like to think the best maps, and the best stories, are honest about their own incompleteness. Old maps sometimes carry the phrase "here be dragons" or simply leave the margins blank, an admission that the surveyor's knowledge had edges, that beyond a certain line the world was unknown. There is more honesty in a blank space than in a confidently drawn lie. A blank space says: I don't know. A trap street says: I know, and I am going to make sure you can't prove otherwise.

---

I have a habit, when I visit a new city, of trying to get lost on purpose. I put the map away and walk without a destination, turning down streets because they look interesting. Sometimes I end up somewhere I could never have planned for: a courtyard with a fountain nobody mentioned, a bookshop with a cat asleep on the counter, a row of houses that seem to lead nowhere. These discoveries feel like gifts precisely because the map did not promise them. The printed city is a starting point. The real city is what you find when you let the lines go slack.

Perhaps this is what the trap street ultimately teaches. Maps are useful, even necessary, but they are not the territory. A map is a model, a set of decisions made by someone with particular purposes and particular blind spots. The best use of a map is to hold it loosely, to check it against what you see, to notice when the world disagrees with it. And when the world disagrees, the right response is curiosity rather than certainty. Maybe the street is missing because the map is wrong. Maybe the street is missing because it was built after the map was printed. Maybe the street was never there at all, and someone wanted to see whether you would notice.

I think of Agloe, the little crossroads that began as a phantom. Today it has a store and people who live there and probably have no idea their town's name was a copyright joke. Its residents are not frauds. They are simply people living in a place that happens to exist, which is more than the original street could ever claim. There is a lesson in that, too: the things we invent can become real if enough people build their lives around them. This is both hopeful and a little alarming. It means that the stories we tell, the categories we draw, and the names we give things can shape the world in ways we did not intend. A map can make a town. A rumor can make a reputation. A repeated claim can make a fact.

So I try, when I can, to be the kind of reader who asks where a thing came from. Not because I expect every street to be a trap, but because the habit of asking keeps the world open. It keeps the blank spaces honest. It reminds me that the lines on any page were drawn by someone, and that I am allowed, even encouraged, to look up from the page and check.

---

If I were to draw my own map, I think it would have a few trap streets of its own. A lane named after a grudge I never quite let go of. A small square that exists only because I once wanted it to. A road that bends toward a house I have never visited but imagine often. These would be my inventions, and I would not be able to tell you which of my beliefs are surveyed and which are invented, since I have built so much of my understanding out of the same materials the mapmaker used: plausible names, confident lines, and the comfortable assumption that what is drawn must be there.

Perhaps that is the real subject of the trap street. It is not really about maps. It is about the gap between the drawing and the land, and about how much of human life happens in that gap. We live by our maps, and we are lost when they fail us. The mapmaker who invented a street was trying to protect his work, but he also created something more interesting: a small reminder that every representation of the world is also a choice, and that choices can be wrong, and that the most important thing a traveler can carry is not a perfect map but the willingness to notice when the road ahead does not match the page.

I hope, when I finally reach the end of my own journey, that I will have left behind more honest maps than I found. Maps with blank spaces where I did not know. Maps with pencil marks where I changed my mind. And, perhaps, a few clearly labeled traps, so that whoever comes after me can see exactly where I was fooling myself, and can walk past the phantom street and onto the real one, which was there all along, waiting to be found.
